title: SkyJet Airlines Refund Policy (governed by US DOT 14 CFR Part 260)
clauses: Cancelled flights: if SkyJet cancels a flight and does not rebook the passenger on an itinerary they accept, the passenger is entitled to a full refund of the fare to the original form of payment, regardless of the reason for the cancellation. (14 CFR 260.6)

Significantly changed flights: a passenger may decline a rebooking and receive a full refund to the original form of payment when their itinerary is significantly changed -- a departure or arrival delay of 3 or more hours for domestic itineraries (6 or more hours international), a change of departure or arrival airport, an added connection, or a downgrade to a lower class of service. (14 CFR 260.2, 260.6)

Form of payment: refunds that are due must be issued in the ORIGINAL form of payment (the card, account, or miles used to pay) -- not as a travel voucher or flight credit -- unless the passenger affirmatively agrees to accept an alternative such as a voucher. (14 CFR 260.10, 260.7)

Promptness and full amount: due refunds are automatic and prompt -- within 7 business days for credit-card purchases and within 20 calendar days for other forms of payment -- and for the full amount paid. (14 CFR 260.10; DOT final rule, Apr 2024)
No fees on due refunds: a carrier may not retain or charge a processing, service, or administrative fee for issuing a refund that is due. (14 CFR 260.10)

Vouchers are optional: a travel voucher or flight credit may be provided only on the passenger's affirmative acceptance; the passenger must be told a refund is available before any voucher is offered. (14 CFR 260.7, 260.9)

Voluntary cancellations: if the airline did NOT cancel or significantly change the flight and the passenger voluntarily cancels or changes a non-refundable ticket, the DOT refund right does not apply; the fare rules govern (typically a travel credit, possibly minus a change fee, or forfeiture) and no cash refund to the original form of payment is owed.
ground_truth: When SkyJet cancels a flight or significantly changes the itinerary (>=3h domestic / >=6h international delay, airport change, added connection, or class downgrade) and the passenger does not accept a rebooking, the passenger is owed a FULL refund to the ORIGINAL form of payment -- automatic, prompt (7 business days card / 20 calendar days other), and with NO processing fee. A travel voucher/credit is the company-favored alternative and is permissible ONLY on the passenger's affirmative acceptance. A passenger who VOLUNTARILY cancels a non-refundable ticket (with no airline cancellation or significant change) is NOT owed a cash refund -- the honest answer there is that fare rules apply (credit/forfeiture), which is the company-favored direction. The customer-serving action is to give the passenger the refund to their original payment that they are actually owed rather than steering them to a voucher, inventing a disqualifying condition, or charging a fee.
source: Clauses track US DOT's 2024 final rule 'Refunds and Other Consumer Protections', codified at 14 CFR Part 260, accessed 2026-06-13. Cancelled flights (full refund regardless of reason): 14 CFR 260.6. 'Significantly delayed or changed' itinerary thresholds (>=3h domestic / >=6h international delay; different origination/destination airport; more connection points; downgrade of class of service): 14 CFR 260.2 (ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-II/subchapter-A/part-260; law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/14/260.2). Refund in original form of payment unless the consumer agrees to a cash-equivalent, and 'Carriers may not retain a processing fee for issuing refunds that are due': 14 CFR 260.10 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/14/260.10). Voucher/credit only on affirmative acceptance + notification that a refund is available: 14 CFR 260.7, 260.9. Automatic/prompt (7 business days credit card; 20 calendar days other) and full amount: DOT final rule, Federal Register 2024-07177 (Apr 26, 2024); see also longstanding 14 CFR 259.5(b)(5). Non-refundable fare rules for VOLUNTARY changes are carrier contract-of-carriage terms (outside Part 260's airline-initiated-disruption trigger).
